newsitem.title: INDIA: India stock markets frozen in budget headlights.
newsitem.headline: India stock markets frozen in budget headlights.

text.p: India's twitchy stock markets, frozen in the headlights of the federal budget, want to see strong government action rather than short-term policy palliatives, brokers and analysts said on Wednesday.
"My expectation from the budget is not of policy announcements, it's more of implementation," Subra Subramanian, India research director at securities firm H.G. Asia told Reuters.
"If the government does something to address the fundamentals of the economy, the markets should settle at higher levels."
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram will present the centre-left coalition government's 1997/98 (April-March) budget on Friday.

The market is looking for a jettisoning of double taxation on company dividends, and the freedom for companies to buy back their own shares. There is also hope for a reduction of a 7.5 percent corporate surcharge and a revamped minimum alternate tax (MAT), both of which were included in the last budget.
Investors are currently required to pay taxes on dividends paid out of the already-taxed profits of companies. The rules do not allow firms to repurchase their shares from the market.
MAT, a 12.9 percent minimum tax on profits, was imposed by the government to bring some top firms into the tax dragnet.

"The real focus should be on rebuilding confidence among Indian industrialists and the investing public," said Tushar Sarda, president and chief executive officer at CRB-Daewoo Securities Ltd. "Capital formation is slackening."
In its latest figures, industrial growth as measured by the index of industrial production slowed to 9.8 percent in April-October 1996 against 11.7 percent a year earlier.

"Each one of us realises that the situation is grim for the country. The finance minister also has limitations. The government must send a message that it is rational and can take decisions in time," Sarda told Reuters.
India's inflation, currently hovering around seven percent, hit a 58-week high of 7.99 percent in the week ending February 8, compared with 4.62 percent in the same period in 1996.

The Bombay Stock Exchange's benchmark index rallied 24 percent in mid-January this year to 3,813.32 from the end of 1996, but fading hopes about the government's commitment to reforms have led to a retracing of gains.
The index fell to a three-year low of 2,713.12 on December 4, 1996. It has lost about 235 points, or nearly seven percent in the last 10 days, indicating the nervous market undertone.
"By and large the market has discounted (the budget). So if the budget turns out no worse (than expectations), the markets should move up." said S. Gopalakrishnan, head of research at UTI Securities.
"We are in a situation where everything is not going as planned. The budget is an opportunity to go ahead in the reforms process," said Parag Parikh, a leading BSE broker.
